doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Bob Scobey's band at Chicago's Blue Note
summary: Scobey's trad band is packed at the Blue Note in 1954; he sees showgirls off to the Vegas casino.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: And the place was swamped. And the second week, the same thing. Because people had heard Scobey’s recordings, and it was the Frisco jazz, and it was strictly, well a little bit advanced from Turk, but they were like traditional — trad.
Yeah, the traditional revival thing going on there.

And a lot of the tunes I knew from a kid, having heard all that stuff on records. And then of course when I got with Scobey why I learned all those tunes, they were a snap, the transition was a snap. So anyhow that was October. So then we came back to San Francisco and so that following May we got a call again. They wanted us for a month. And during that month there was a woman who lived in Chicago who was an ex-showgirl from Seattle and Ernie Lewis the pianist, I got him the job with Scobey. He knew her, so one day we got a call from her says, “Come on ride out to the airport with me.” “Oh yeah, okay.” So we met her at her house, there were two cars, and they were loaded with showgirls. And we went to the airport in Chicago. They were going out to Vegas. They were going to be the showgirls for that casino out there. And it was all the talk in Chicago about this casino. Because you know the black community, we knew about the conditions in Vegas, in fact in the state of Nevada. So this was monumental. It was a big thing. So we got to see the girls off.
